Keywords: That, Kenji, Takezo

outputs.L1:
That boy, Kenji Takezo—the champion breath-holder—lost his title this year to Mack Stanton, a retired truck driver new to the area. The contest was held at the town swimming pool. Thirty-five participants inhaled deeply all at once and submerged themselves in the depths. The competition continued into twilight. One by one, each person surfaced, gasping for air.

Kenji was the town favorite. We wanted him to win again. He had trained so hard; it was the only real talent he had, other than surfing and making trouble. When he surfaced second to last, gulping the night air and then vomiting water, we were disappointed. He had been doing so well, his lucky twenty-pound brick cradled in his lap to keep him down.

But Mack, the trucker, was too good. He read comic books aloud underwater, and from the bleachers, we watched his laughter burst above him. Kenji saw it too. No one had ever read to him—not even his mother—and he wanted to hear what was being read, what his opponent found so funny.
outputs.L2:
The town’s breath-holding crown had belonged to Kenji Takezo, but this year he surrendered it to Mack Stanton, a retired trucker who had only recently moved nearby.

The competition took place in the municipal pool. Thirty-five contestants filled their lungs together, then sank beneath the surface. Dusk arrived while the event was still underway. Gradually, the competitors emerged one after another, gasping for air.

Everyone rooted for Kenji to repeat his victory. He had practiced relentlessly, and aside from surfing and causing trouble, holding his breath was his only genuine gift. So when he came up next to last—swallowing the night air before throwing up water—we felt let down. Until then, he had seemed likely to win. His fortunate twenty-pound brick rested in his lap, weighing him down and helping him remain submerged.

Mack, however, proved unbeatable. Underwater, the former truck driver read comic books out loud. From the bleachers, we could see his laughter bubbling to the surface.

Kenji noticed it as well. No one had ever read to him, not even his mother. Curious about the words and eager to understand what his rival found so amusing, he abandoned his chance at the title and rose to listen.

Kenji Takezo had long been the town’s favorite breath-holding champion, and nearly everyone expected him to defend his title at the annual competition. This year, however, he faced an unlikely challenger: Mack Stanton, a retired truck driver who had only recently moved to the area.

Thirty-five contestants gathered in the town swimming pool and submerged themselves at the starting signal. As twilight drew near, they rose one by one, gasping for air, until only Kenji and Mack remained beneath the surface. Kenji had trained relentlessly for the event. He had even brought his lucky twenty-pound brick, which he clutched to keep himself firmly underwater. Despite all his preparation, he finally surfaced second to last and immediately vomited up a mouthful of pool water.

Mack claimed the title in a far less conventional fashion. While submerged, he calmly read comic books aloud, occasionally laughing so loudly that bursts of sound and bubbles broke the surface. It was this laughter that ultimately defeated Kenji. Distracted and intensely curious, Kenji strained to hear the story. No one had ever read aloud to him before—not even his mother—and he became desperate to discover what Mack found so funny. In the end, curiosity overcame determination, and Kenji surfaced, leaving the newcomer to become the town’s new champion.
outputs.L4:
Every summer, the town held its breath-holding contest at the old quarry pond. Folding chairs crowded the bank, children climbed the willow trees for a better view, and nearly everyone arrived certain of the outcome. Kenji Takezo had won for six years in a row.

Kenji was a broad-shouldered man with a solemn face and a reputation for treating every contest as a matter of honor. He trained before sunrise, plunging into the cold pond with a twenty-pound brick clutched against his chest. When people asked how he could remain underwater so long, he only shrugged.

“You decide not to breathe,” he would say.

This year, however, a newcomer entered the contest. Mack Stanton had moved into town in the spring, bringing with him a battered suitcase, a stack of comic books, and the habit of talking to anyone who happened to be nearby. He was thin, cheerful, and so unimpressed by Kenji’s reputation that the townspeople assumed he must be foolish.

On the morning of the contest, Mack appeared at the pond wearing a striped bathing suit and carrying a rolled-up comic book.

The judge frowned. “What’s that for?”

“Entertainment,” Mack replied.

“You can’t read underwater.”

“I can try.”

The crowd laughed. Kenji did not. He stood at the edge of the pond holding his brick, his expression as hard as the stone itself.

The rules were simple. At the sound of the bell, each contestant would submerge. Anyone whose head broke the surface was out. The last person underwater would be declared the winner.

A dozen contestants lined the bank. The judge raised his hand and rang the bell.

They plunged in.

At first the pond was a confusion of bubbles and kicking feet. Then the water settled. One by one, contestants rose gasping to the surface. The crowd cheered each appearance, though everyone watched for Kenji.

Beneath the water, Kenji sat on the muddy bottom with the brick in his lap. He closed his eyes and counted his heartbeats. He ignored the pressure in his chest. He ignored the cold creeping through his arms. Winning required discipline, and discipline meant shutting out everything else.

Then he heard a faint, garbled voice.

Kenji opened his eyes.

A few yards away, Mack sat cross-legged on the bottom. The comic book was open in his hands, its pages wavering in the water. He was reading aloud—or attempting to. Most of the words emerged as bubbles, but now and then a phrase could be understood.

“The Shadow Falcon… escaped the moon prison…”

Kenji stared at him.

Mack turned the page with great difficulty. The paper had already begun to soften. He continued the story, puffing out words between tightly pressed lips.

Above them, another contestant surfaced.

Mack pointed to a picture of a masked hero swinging from an airship. He widened his eyes dramatically and supplied the villain’s voice. The sound was ridiculous: a deep underwater gurgle accompanied by a stream of silver bubbles.

Kenji looked away. This was a contest, not a performance.

Still, he wondered what happened next.

He focused again on his heartbeat. His lungs had begun to ache, but he knew the ache well. He could endure it longer than anyone. Yet Mack kept reading. The Shadow Falcon had apparently lost the key to the moon prison. A mechanical sea monster was approaching. Someone named Captain Thunder had been betrayed.

Another head burst through the surface.

Only three contestants remained.

Mack turned a page too quickly, tearing it in half. He stared at the ruined sheet in exaggerated horror. Then he tried to fit the pieces together, got them backward, and began reading the panels in the wrong order.

Kenji’s mouth twitched.

Mack noticed. He pointed triumphantly at Kenji, as if catching him in the act of enjoying himself. Then Mack resumed the tale with even greater enthusiasm, acting out a battle between the Shadow Falcon and the mechanical sea monster. He shook the comic book for thunder, waved one hand like a tentacle, and crossed his eyes when the monster was struck.

A laugh rose inside Kenji before he could stop it.

He clamped his lips shut, but laughter was more difficult to contain than breath. His shoulders shook. A bubble escaped his nose.

Mack grinned.

The remaining contestant surfaced, coughing and splashing. The people onshore erupted in applause. Now only Kenji and Mack were left.

Kenji knew what he had to do. He had survived longer than this in practice. Mack had wasted precious air reading and laughing. If Kenji waited a little longer, victory would be his again.

But Mack pointed to the final panel of the comic.

The page was blurred, the ink dissolving into blue and red clouds. Kenji could not make out the words. Mack began to read them, but his voice had weakened. His cheeks were puffed, and his hands trembled.

Kenji leaned closer.

Mack held the comic between them. In the last picture, the Shadow Falcon and Captain Thunder stood together on the wreckage of the moon prison. One speech balloon remained just clear enough to read.

Kenji wanted to know what it said. More than that, he wanted to hear Mack say it. He wanted to hear the ridiculous voices without the water swallowing half the words. He wanted to laugh openly instead of hiding behind a fixed expression.

For years, people had admired Kenji’s strength from a respectful distance. They praised him, feared him, and left him alone. He had mistaken their distance for honor because that was easier than admitting it felt like loneliness.

Mack tapped the final speech balloon.

Kenji released the brick.

He kicked toward the light and broke the surface with a great gasp.

The crowd fell silent. Kenji Takezo had surfaced second to last. For the first time in six years, he had lost.

A moment later, Mack emerged beside him, choking, laughing, and holding the remains of the comic book above his head.

The judge declared Mack the new champion. The crowd cheered, but Kenji hardly seemed to hear. He swam toward Mack.

“What did the last panel say?” Kenji asked.

Mack wiped water from his eyes. “You came up before the ending?”

“I came up for the ending.”

Mack studied him, then smiled.

Together they climbed onto the bank. Mack spread the soggy comic across a sun-warmed rock and read the final line aloud. It was a terrible joke about moon cheese.

Kenji laughed anyway—loudly enough to startle the judge and silence the crowd. Then Mack laughed, too, and before long the whole bank joined them.

By the following summer, Kenji had stopped training alone. He still carried the twenty-pound brick into the pond, but Mack came with him, armed with a fresh stack of comic books sealed in waterproof covers.

Kenji never again held the town record for staying underwater.

He did, however, become famous for being the hardest man in town to make laugh—and for laughing longer than anyone once he began.
outputs.L5:
“That mountain looks impossible to climb,” Kenji said, staring at the snow-covered peak.

Takezo tightened the rope around his waist and smiled. “That is why we must try.”

Together, they began the ascent. The wind grew stronger, and every step tested their courage. Kenji wanted to turn back, but Takezo reminded him that strength was not the absence of fear—it was the decision to continue despite it.

By sunset, they reached the summit. Looking across the glowing horizon, Kenji finally understood: the mountain had not been their greatest obstacle. It had been the doubt within themselves.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about a small-town breath-holding contest in which the local champion loses to a retired truck driver who reads comic books underwater.
counterfactuals.output:
Every August, the town filled the courthouse pool  
with water borrowed from the moon.

The mayor wore his ceremonial flippers.  
The baker sold blue loaves.  
Children pressed their faces to the glass  
and practiced becoming ghosts.

For eleven years, Milo Vane had been champion.  
He could hold his breath through a church bell,  
a marriage, and the slow apology of rain.  
Underwater, he sat cross-legged and calm,  
his lungs two locked suitcases.

Then came Earl Pike, retired truck driver,  
knees ruined by Nebraska, beard full of road dust.  
He entered wearing a faded swimsuit  
and carrying a stack of comic books  
sealed in sandwich bags.

The whistle blew.

Milo descended like a coin in a wishing well.  
Earl sank beside him, opened *The Astonishing Moth-Man*,  
and began to read.

Above them, the town waited.  
A dog barked once and reconsidered.  
The clock tower coughed up twelve black birds.  
Milo counted heartbeats, then sins, then spoons.

Earl turned a page.

In the green silence, speech bubbles rose around him:  
ZAP!  
BEWARE!  
TO BE CONTINUED!

His eyes moved peacefully behind his spectacles.  
He had driven forty years through storms  
that tried to erase Ohio,  
through nights when the highway unrolled  
like a tongue from the mouth of God.  
He knew how to live inside a long distance.

At three minutes, Milo saw his dead grandfather  
waving from a submerged barbershop.

At four, he saw every door in town open at once.

At five, he burst upward, dragging the whole sky  
into his mouth.

The crowd cheered, then remembered Earl.

Far below, the old truck driver read on,  
one hand tucked beneath his belly,  
the other holding open a universe  
where no one needed air  
and heroes always returned by the final panel.

When Earl finally surfaced, the moon-water  
poured from his sleeves. He blinked at the mayor.

“Good issue,” he said.

They crowned him with a wreath of pondweed.  
Milo shook his hand. Somewhere underground,  
a diesel engine dreamed of whales.

That night, the town slept with windows open,  
and everyone’s breath wandered out  
to stand beside the road,  
thumb raised,  
waiting for Earl to take it somewhere impossible.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a free-verse narrative featuring Kenji Takezo, a troubled young surfer whose only real talent is holding his breath, and Mack Stanton, an eccentric newcomer who defeats him at the town swimming pool.
counterfactuals.output:
Kenji Takezo knew the underside of waves—  
the green cathedral,  
the tumble of sand and shell,  
the long, muffled thunder  
that frightened other boys back toward shore.

He was not graceful on a board.

He rose too late,  
leaned too hard,  
fell from every clean face  
the ocean offered him.

On land, he was worse.

Teachers called him distracted.  
His mother called him unreachable.  
The older surfers at Kurohama Point  
called him Driftwood,  
something carried without direction.

But Kenji could hold his breath.

Two minutes beneath the pier.  
Three in the quarry pond.  
Long enough for his friends  
to stop laughing  
and begin to worry.

Underwater,  
he did not hear his father’s slammed doors  
or the unpaid phone ringing  
in the kitchen.

His heart slowed.

The world became  
a blue room  
with no questions.

Then Mack Stanton arrived in town  
wearing a red wool coat in June,  
driving a van painted  
with silver moons.

He claimed he had crossed deserts barefoot,  
trained dolphins for the navy,  
and once slept in a church bell  
during a thunderstorm.

No one believed him.

He was forty, perhaps sixty,  
with white-blond hair,  
one gold tooth,  
and goggles thick as jar bottoms.

At the municipal pool  
he swam each morning  
in crooked spirals,  
sometimes backward,  
sometimes with an orange balanced on his forehead.

Kenji watched from the bleachers.

“You’re the boy who lives underwater,”  
Mack said one day.

Kenji shrugged.

“I hear you’re unbeatable.”

“I don’t race.”

“Neither does winter,” Mack said,  
“but it catches everyone.”

By noon the rumor had spread.

They stood at opposite ends  
of the deep lane  
while lifeguards pretended  
not to be interested.

The contest was simple:

sink,  
stay,  
surface last.

Kenji filled his lungs  
until his ribs ached.

Mack merely smiled,  
removed his gold tooth,  
and placed it carefully  
beside the orange.

They slipped below.

At first Kenji was calm.

Chlorine light trembled  
across the tiles.  
The crowd became a blur of legs,  
shadows cut off at the knees.

One minute.

Two.

Kenji folded himself  
at the bottom,  
hands around his shins.

Across the lane  
Mack sat cross-legged,  
eyes open,  
his hair floating upward  
like pale fire.

Three minutes.

Kenji’s chest began to knock.

He thought of the ocean,  
how it never asked permission  
before breaking.

He thought of his father leaving,  
his mother counting coins,  
the surfboard hidden behind the shed  
with its nose split open.

Still Mack did not move.

Four minutes—

or a lifetime measured  
in blue squares.

Pain climbed Kenji’s throat.

His body became  
an animal trapped inside him,  
kicking at the door.

He looked at Mack.

The old man lifted one finger  
and pointed upward.

Not a taunt.

An invitation.

Kenji shook his head.

Mack pointed again,  
then pressed a palm  
to his own heart.

Kenji understood  
and hated him for it.

He pushed off the bottom,  
burst into air,  
and dragged it down  
with a broken, sobbing gasp.

The crowd shouted.

A moment later  
Mack surfaced quietly,  
as if waking from a pleasant dream.

“You cheated,” Kenji coughed.

“Probably,” Mack said,  
returning the gold tooth to his mouth.

“How?”

“By not needing to win.”

The words struck harder  
than defeat.

Kenji left the pool,  
shoved through the laughing boys,  
and ran until the streets  
gave way to dunes.

At Kurohama Point  
the evening swell was rising.

He paddled out  
on the cracked board.

The first wave threw him.

The second folded him  
into darkness.

He held his breath by instinct,  
waiting for the old blue room  
to close around him.

But Mack’s finger appeared  
in his mind,  
pointing upward.

So Kenji surfaced.

He climbed back on.

Again,  
and again,  
and again—

until dusk laid violet hands  
across the water.

At last a small wave lifted him.

Kenji stood badly,  
knees shaking,  
arms wild.

For three brief seconds  
he traveled with it—  
not beneath,  
not hidden,  
not holding anything in—

and on the beach,  
beside a van painted with moons,  
Mack Stanton raised an orange  
like a tiny sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Tell a darkly humorous story from the perspective of townspeople watching their favorite contestant lose an underwater endurance competition. Include thirty-five participants, a twenty-pound lucky brick, and an unexpectedly poignant ending.
counterfactuals.output:
All thirty-five participants went into the reservoir at noon, each clutching a twenty-pound lucky brick.

The rules of the annual Saint Ormund Underwater Endurance Competition were simple: hold your brick, stay beneath the surface, and be the last to come up.

In retrospect, simplicity was not the same thing as wisdom.

We townspeople lined the dam with picnic baskets and funeral umbrellas. The mayor fired the starting pistol, though no one had explained why a firearm was necessary near thirty-five nervous people carrying masonry. Our favorite contestant, Edgar Vale, kissed his brick before sinking.

Edgar was easy to love. He delivered milk, remembered birthdays, and once apologized to a lamppost after walking into it. His brick was painted gold and named Patricia, after his late wife.

“Lucky Patricia,” he called it.

“She certainly wasn’t lucky the first time,” muttered the undertaker, who had buried the original.

The reservoir swallowed everyone with thirty-five soft plunks.

At first, the surface bubbled merrily. We cheered. Children waved little flags bearing Edgar’s face. The brass band played “Sink or Swim,” which the council had chosen without fully considering the title.

After one minute, three contestants surfaced.

After two, eleven more burst upward, gasping and swearing. One had lost his brick and was disqualified. Another had found two bricks and demanded extra credit.

At four minutes, only eight remained below.

At five, the rescue divers began putting on their masks. This was considered poor sportsmanship by the traditionalists.

At six minutes, the defending champion emerged, blue-lipped and furious. He slapped the water and shouted, “There’s a shopping trolley down there!”

We applauded. The reservoir had not seen a shop in forty years, so this seemed remarkable.

Then there were two: Edgar and a visiting accountant named Miss Bell, whose expression before submerging had suggested she regarded oxygen as an unnecessary expense.

The town fell silent.

Seven minutes.

Eight.

At nine minutes, Miss Bell surfaced, inhaled half the sky, and was declared the winner.

We waited for Edgar.

The band lowered its instruments. The mayor removed his hat. The undertaker checked his watch with professional discretion.

Then Edgar’s golden brick broke the surface.

A rescue diver followed, hauling Edgar by the collar. He was coughing, alive, and furious.

“I dropped Patricia,” he wheezed.

The diver held up the brick. Tied around it was a length of rotten rope—and caught in that rope was a small metal box.

Inside were thirty-five letters, yellowed but dry in waxed envelopes. They had been written decades earlier by soldiers from our town before they left for a war from which most never returned. Someone had hidden them in the old church wall; the wall had later been demolished and dumped into the reservoir. Patricia, in her descent, had snagged the box from the ruins.

The competition was forgotten.

That evening, families gathered in the town hall while the mayor read the names on the envelopes. Some belonged to grandparents we remembered only from photographs. Some belonged to houses now empty. One letter was addressed simply:

**To the child I have not met yet.**

It was Edgar’s father’s handwriting.

Edgar sat beneath the championship banner, wrapped in a blanket, Patricia on his knees. He opened the letter with trembling fingers. No one laughed when he began to cry, though we had laughed at nearly everything else that day.

Miss Bell gave him the winner’s medal.

“You stayed under too long,” she said.

Edgar held the old letter to his chest.

“Not long enough,” he replied.

The next year, we replaced the underwater endurance competition with a cake raffle.

No one drowned, but three people developed diabetes, and somehow that felt more civilized.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented, dreamlike poem about loneliness and competition. The protagonist should surface second to last in a breath-holding contest because he becomes distracted by an opponent reading aloud underwater.
counterfactuals.output:
At the bottom of the municipal pool  
the lane ropes grow red berries.

Seven of us descend  
with our lungs locked—  
small suitcases  
no one admits are empty.

Above: judges, stopwatches,  
mothers blurred into weather.

Below: competition becomes religion.  
Elbows of light.  
Knees folded like questions.

I count my heartbeats  
until the boy beside me  
opens a book.

Underwater.

He reads aloud—  
not words, exactly,  
but silver animals  
escaping his mouth:

*Once there was a house  
with only one chair—*

The pages do not dissolve.  
His voice moves through me  
like a train heard from a lonely room.

I forget the prize.  
I forget the surface  
is where breathing happens.

One by one, the others rise,  
their bodies dark commas  
returning to the sentence of air.

Still he reads.

*Once there was a door  
that waited all winter—*

I follow each bubble upward,  
jealous of its perfect loneliness.

At last my chest becomes  
a fist knocking from inside.

I surface second to last—  
gasping beneath the scoreboard,  
defeated by a story  
I could not hear.

The reader comes up after me.

He wins.

No one asks  
what the book said.

We stand apart in our wet skins  
while the crowd applauds  
the longest silence.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary prose poem with unusual capitalization and short, broken lines about a champion breath holder named Kenji who has never been read to—not even by his mother—and loses his title after wanting to hear a rival’s comic book.
counterfactuals.output:
Kenji could keep  
the sea  
inside him.

whole Minutes  
folded their blue wings  
in his chest.

crowds counted backward.

his Mother watched  
with hands like closed books.

No one  
had ever read to him—

not the woman  
who tucked silence  
around his bed,

not the teachers  
who mistook quiet  
for knowing.

Then came the Rival,  
bright-capped,  
carrying a comic book  
creased by laughter.

Beneath the tournament lights  
Kenji sank.

One minute.  
two.

At the pool’s edge  
the Rival began  
to read aloud:

a moon exploded.  
a hero fell upward.  
the speech balloons  
opened their little white mouths.

Kenji heard  
WORDS  
becoming doors.

He wanted the next panel.

He wanted  
the voice  
to keep happening.

So the champion rose early,  
bursting through water  
with a child’s first breath—

and lost.

The judges raised  
another name.

Kenji did not hear it.

He was listening  
to the page turn,

that small thunder,

that Motherless  
miracle.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
